              COMMENTS OF THE TEXAS BITCOIN & GRID ALLIANCE
                     ON PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC § 25.521


                                     I.       INTRODUCTION

       The Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance ("TBGA") respectfully submits these comments in
response to Commission Staff's proposal for publication ("PFP") issued July 30, 2026, published
in the August 14 , 2026 issue of the Texas Register, in Project No . 58482 , concerning proposed
new 16 Texas Administrative Code ("TAC") § 25.521, Large Load Demand Management Service
("LLDMS"). Comments are due September 4,2026. Therefore, these comments are timely filed.
The proposed rule is intended to implement Public Utility Regulatory Act ("PURA") § 39.170,
enacted by Senate Bill ("SB") 6 during the 89~h Regular Legislative Session.

       TBGA is a Texas-based trade association representing innovative companies-both
established incumbents and entrepreneurial new entrants-working to advance mutually beneficial
market designs and policies. Its objective is to create clear regulatory pathways for businesses
whose technologies and operating models can measurably improve reliability and affordability for
residential ratepayers. Bitcoin miners form TBGA's founding member base and provide its
foundational operating experience, but they do not limit its broader purpose.

       TBGA's members share a particular commitment to addressing the collective-action
problem facing residential ratepayers. Residential customers bear the reliability consequences and
financial costs of many grid decisions, yet their dispersed interests and limited specialized
resources make sustained participation in complex utility and market-design proceedings
impractical. TBGA seeks to help fill that gap by supporting reforms that measurably strengthen
reliability and improve affordability-and by opposing structures that shift private costs, risks, or
infrastructure burdens onto Texas households.

       TBGA also has a direct and substantial interest in this rulemaking. Its membership includes
companies operating and developing multiple gigawatts of transmission-voltage load across


            Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 1 of 22
 multiple sites in the ERCOT region. TBGA members include entities that meet the proposed
definition of "large load customef' in § 25.521(b)(2), entities developing transmission-voltage
load that may be subject to the firm-load-shed requirement in proposed § 25.521(a)(1), and
prospective LLDMS participants proposed under § 25.521(a)(2). The proposed rule therefore
directly affects TBGA members' interconnection requirements, operating obligations, capital
investments, eligibility to provide demand reductions, and compensation for verified reliability
services.
          TBGA members bring demonstrated, fleet-scale experience operating the type of
controllable computational demand. Certain computational loads provide granular demand
reduction. As one public example, Riot Platforms publicly reported curtailing more than 95% of
its power usage during peak-demand periods in August 2023.1 That reported operating history
illustrates both the potential reliability value of flexible load, but it should not substitute for
verification of an individual facility's capability.

          TBGA therefore supports a rigorous, technology-neutral framework under which any large
load operating characteristic relied upon for reliability must be physical, measurable, observable,
tested, verifiable, and enforceable. Properly designed, § 25.521 can distinguish uncontrolled load
loss, which may create reliability risk, from deliberate and coordinated demand reduction that can
reduce the need for firm load shed affecting other customers. It can also ensure that participating
resources receive appropriate compensation for verified services without duplicate compensation
or avoidable cost shifting.

          That approach is consistent with the Legislature' s design. PURA §39.170(a) expressly
requires the serving electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally
owned utility to "confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated
manner," while §39. 170(b) requires ERCOT to develop a competitively procured reliability
service for qualifying large loads. The Senate Research Center bill analysis likewise identifies
"protecting residential customers from outages by requiring large loads to share the load shed
obligation during times of shortage" as one of Senate Bill 6's principal objectives.2 The final rule

https://www.riotplatforms.com/riot-announces-august-2023-production-and-operations-updates/.
2 PURA § 39 . 170 ( a)-(b ); See also Senate Research Center, S . B . 6 Bill Analysis at 1 , 5 ( Aug . 5 , 2025 ).

 should give effect to those directives without expanding either subsection beyond the authority the
Legislature conferred.

       These comments follow the order of the proposed rule, respond to each question posed by
Commission Staff for comment, and provide recommended revisions to proposed § 25.521. A
standalone executive summary is also included as the final page of this filing.

                         II.   SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS

       TBGA respectfully submits proposed rule text in Section V that would implement the
recommendations discussed in Sections III and IV, and asks that the Commission adopt those
provisions in its final rule. Specifically, the Alliance recommends the following interrelated
modifications:

R-1.   Amend § 25.521(a)(1) to add minimum statewide requirements that carry forward PURA
       §39.170(a)' s express customer-coordination mandate and require covered curtailment
       capability to be installed, commissioned, tested, observable where technically necessary,
       periodically verified, and implemented through enforceable through an enforceable
       instrument.

R-2.   Amend §25.521(a)(1) to establish an objective baseline for pre-existing load and clarify
       that that a discrete increment of load first energized or otherwise made available to take
       service after December 31, 2025 is subject to subsection (a)(1), without automatically
       subj ecting pre-existing load at the same site to the new requirement .

R-3.   Where covered incremental load and pre-existing load are served behind the same
       controlling device used for load shed, permit the customer to elect either (1) to place the
       pre-existing load into interruptible standing so that all load behind the controlling device
       may be curtailed during firm load shed, or (2) to establish the control equipment necessary
       to curtail the covered incremental load independently; and direct ERCOT to evaluate and
       report on whole-site coverage for circumstances the election does not resolve.

R-4.   Apply § 25.521(c)(2) consistent with PURA §39.170(b)(3) and preserve the statutory
       exclusions for customers that curtail in response to the wholesale price of electricity or
       participate in another reliability or ancillary service, and narrowly tailor any additional
       exclusions to prevent duplicate compensation or conflicting obligations for the same
       megawatts in the same interval, without technology-based eligibility screens

R-5.   Replace the automatic offer-rejection provision in § 25.521(d)(3)(B)(iii) with a cross-
       reference to the compliance framework in § 25.521(g), and require ERCOT's compliance
       criteria to address materiality, notice and an opportunity to respond and cure where
       appropriate, partial performance and documented circumstances outside the customer' s




            Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 3 of 22
        reasonable control, proportionate consequences, suspension and reinstatement, and a
       defined dispute process.

R-6.   Amend § 25.521(f)(1)(C) and (f)(1)(D) to make payment mandatory ("must receive") for
       a customer that performs, and specify the quantity basis on which the availability payment
       is calculated.

R-7.   Add a new § 25.521(f)(5) providing that LLDMS compensation is available only for
       demand reduction that ERCOT is not otherwise entitled to receive at the time of
       deployment, preserving the distinction between the uncompensated firm-load-shed
       backstop under subsection (a)(1) and the compensated LLDMS product without
       disqualifying loads that carry both.

R-8.   Add § 25.521(e)(4) to address recall and restoration as a coordinated procedure, including
       sequencing, ramping, and load rebound, consistent with the rules developed under
       subsection (a).

R-9.   Rationalize LLDMS with the Emergency Response Service (ERS) under 16 TAC § 25.507.
       The two programs procure overlapping emergency demand response under separate annual
       caps-$54 million for LLDMS and $75 million (up to $100 million with renewal authority)
       for ERS. The Commission should determine whether ERS should be consolidated into
       LLDMS, maintained at a significantly reduced level, or phased out as LLDMS enrollment
       grows, and at a minimum should adopt new § 25.521(j) requiring ERCOT to evaluate the
       two programs j ointly each year and recommend reductions in duplicative procurement and
       cost.

R-10. Adopt TBGA's responses to the Commission's four questions (Section IV):

       i.        Compensate verified availability as a percentage of the real-time energy price and
                 address documented, non-price-responsive temporary unavailability without
                 creating an exception to PURA §39.170(b)(3);

       ii.       Treat the annual budget as an output of the § 25.521(d)(2) risk assessment with full
                 transparency on its consumption;

       iii.      Make the weekly forecast the primary procurement trigger, feasible on short
                 timelines because LLDMS is a standardized, fully defined product; and

       iv.       Authorize transmission-emergency deployment only as a last resort after other
                 management mechanisms are exhausted, never for planned outages, with
                 conforming amendments making the defined term operative.

                          III.    COMMENTS ON PROPOSED § 25.521

A.      §25.521(a)(1) - The required rule must produce a verified operational capability, not
        a paper commitment. (R-1)

        Proposed § 25.521(a)(1) directs ERCOT to ensure that each electric cooperative,
transmission and distribution utility ("TDU"), and municipally owned utility ("MOU") serving a
transmission-voltage customer develops a rule--including installation of any necessary equipment
or technology before interconnection-to allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The
proposed text faithfully restates the statutory directive in PURA § 39.170 but stops there: it
specifies no minimum content for the rule, no testing or verification requirement, and no
mechanism by which the obligation becomes enforceable against the customer. As drafted,
subsection (a)(1) permits full compliance through a rule that exists only on paper.

        The operational stakes are concrete. In February 2021, ERCOT directed firm load shed that
reached approximately 20,000 MW and was sustained for days, executed almost entirely by
opening distribution feeders serving homes and small businesses. A single 300 MW transmission-
voltage load with tested, telemetered curtailment capability represents one dispatch instruction
with confirmed effect. Shedding the same 300 MW through rotating outages requires opening on
the order of sixty distribution feeders at roughly 5 MW each, interrupting tens of thousands of
premises-including residences-in the middle of an emergency. Every megawatt of dependable,
controllable large load curtailment directly displaces feeder-level rotating outages. That is the
reliability benefit subsection (a)(1) exists to secure, and it is realized only ifthe capability actually
works when called.

        The specific problem is this: if ERCOT and the serving utility do not know what they will
actually get from a transmission-connected load when it is instructed to curtail, they must back up
that load' s response with load they can shed with certainty-residential and commercial
distribution feeders. A curtailment commitment that cannot be confirmed through tested
communications and telemetry cannot be counted toward the shed obligation, so the operator must
plan as though it will not perform. In that condition, the nominally curtailable large load has
displaced nothing; the feeders carry the obligation anyway. Installation, commissioning, end-to-
end testing, and telemetry are what convert a large load' s curtailment capability from an




            Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 5 of 22
 assumption the operator must hedge into a resource the operator can count-and every countable
megawatt is a megawatt of rotating outages avoided.

        TBGA recommends the Commission adopt the following implementation principle: any
large load operating characteristic upon which ERCOT relies for reliability should be measurable,
observable, testable, verifiable, and enforceable. The Commission should establish the reliability
obligation; ERCOT and the serving utility should establish the engineering requirements; and the
customer should demonstrate and maintain performance. The Commission need not prescribe a
communications architecture, response time, protection setting, or facility design-those decisions
belong within ERCOT's and the serving utility' s technical authority. But the final rule should
require a sufficiently complete framework that ERCOT can determine, for each covered load: how
much load can be reduced; under what conditions; how the instruction will be issued and received;
how quickly and reliably the load will respond; whether the reduction can be sustained; how
performance will be measured; how the load will be restored safely; and what occurs when the
capability is not installed, tested, maintained, or performed.

        Accordingly, TBGA recommends that § 25.521(a) be amended to require that each
requirement developed under subsection (a)(1) include, as appropriate to the facility and system
need:
        •   Pre-interconnection readiness - installation, commissioning, and operational
            readiness of the necessary equipment or technology before covered load is
            interconnected or expanded capacity is energized;

        •   Communications and controls - defined primary and backup communications paths,
            designated contacts, command acknowledgment procedures, and controls sufficient to
            execute the required curtailment reliably;

        •   Telemetry and metering - telemetry, event records, and metering sufficient for
            ERCOT and the serving utility to observe and verify performance where technically
            necessary;
            Testing and certification - initial end-to-end testing before service is made available,
            including communications, actual or simulated load reduction, response behavior,
            telemetry validation, and restoration;

        •   Continuing verification - periodic retesting, recertification, event reporting, and
            material-change reporting sufficient to ensure the capability remains dependable;




            Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 6 of 22
        •   Controlled restoration - procedures addressing recall, sequencing, ramping, and
           load rebound (see Section III.E below);

       •   Binding implementation - the customer obligation must be made effective through
           the applicable tariff, interconnection agreement, service agreement, or other authorized
           instrument; an ERCOT rule or customer acknowledgment alone should not be
           presumed enforceable; and

       •   Notice, cure, and proportionate consequences - notice, a reasonable opportunity to
           cure where appropriate, retesting, and lawful consequences for continued failure, which
           may include withholding, limiting, or suspending unenergized or expanded capacity
           until the required capability is demonstrated.

       Proposed rule text implementing this recommendation appears in Section V as new §
25.521(a)(3).

B.     §25.521(a)(1) - The applicability provision should codify                         an    objective
       grandfathering baseline and a clear expansion standard. (R-2, R-3)

       Proposed § 25.521(a)(1) applies to "a load interconnected after December 31, 2025." The
text does not define "interconnected"-agreement execution, energization, or some other
milestone-and does not state how the rule applies to incremental capacity added after that date at
a site that previously took service. The statutory text warrants a careful distinction. PURA
§39.170(a) uses the date-limited phrase "a load interconnected after December 31, 2025," while
PURA §37.0561(c) separately and expressly addresses a "new or expanded interconnection." The
final rule therefore should not assume that any post-2025 expansion automatically brings all pre-
existing load at the site within §39.170(a). At the same time, a discrete increment of load first
energized or otherwise made available to take service after December 31, 2025 can reasonably be
treated as load interconnected after that date. The rule should draw that line expressly.

       A concrete example illustrates both the ambiguity and its resolution. A 150 MW
transmission-voltage site interconnected in 2024 receives approval for and energizes an additional
250 MW in 2027. The better reading is that the newly energized 250 MW can be treated as post-
2025 load; the statutory text does not, however, clearly make the pre-existing 150 MW subj ect to
subsection (a)(1) solely because it shares the same site. Now add the engineering reality: if the 250
MW expansion shares a main breaker, protection scheme, or common facilities with the pre-
existing 150 MW, the serving utility physically cannot curtail the new load without also curtailing
the old. The applicability question is therefore not academic; it determines how the Legislature's



            Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 7 of 22
 prospective firm-load-shed requirement applies when pre-existing and later-added load share
facilities.

         TBGA recommends a two-part standard. First, the rule should identify an obj ective
baseline for pre-existing load-e.g.,the maximum load that, as of December 31, 2025, was both
authorized under an effective interconnection agreement, service agreement, tariff, utility-
approved service level, or comparable legally effective instrument and energized or otherwise
available to take service. This avoids extending pre-existing treatment to speculative, unapproved,
abandoned, or unenergized capacity merely because it appeared in an earlier request or
development plan.

         Second, a discrete increment of transmission-voltage load first energized or otherwise
made available to take service after December 31, 2025 should comply with subsection (a)(1)
before that increment is energized or made available. This approach gives effect to the statutory
date limitation while preserving prospective application to later-added load.

         Third, where the covered incremental load and pre-existing load served behind the same
controlling device used for load shed, the rule should require the customer to elect either (1) to
place its pre-existing load into interruptible standing, so that allload behind the controlling device
may be curtailed during firm load shed, or (2) to establish the control equipment, protection, and
metering necessary to curtail the covered incremental load independently. Either election makes
the covered increment controllable without automatically extending subsection (a)(1) to pre-
existing load. Cost responsibility for any additional equipment should be determined under
otherwise applicable law, tariffs, and agreements rather than prescribed categorically in this rule

         Fourth, the Commission should direct ERCOT to evaluate whole-site coverage for
circumstances the election does not resolve. Whole-site treatment may present operational benefits
where pre-existing and incremental load cannot be reliably separated, but mandatory whole-site
coverage of pre-existing load is not an express requirement of PURA §39.170(a). Section
39.170(a) uses the date-limited phrase "a load interconnected after December 31, 2025," while
PURA § 37.0561 uses distinct language addressing new or expanded interconnections and total
load at a single site. The Commission should therefore develop the record on any residual whole-
site issue and identify a clear statutory basis before extending the subsection (a)(1) requirement to
pre-existing load.



              Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 8 of 22
 C.      § 25.521(c)(2) - Eligibility should be defined by the service, not by the resource. (R-
        4)

        Proposed § 25.521(c)(2) lists nine categories of programs and services whose participants
are ineligible for LLDMS. PURA §39.170(b)(3) itself requires two exclusions: customers that
curtail in response to the wholesale price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, and customers
that otherwise participate in a different reliability or ancillary service. THE ALLIANCE does not
seek to narrow those statutory prohibitions. For the additional categories proposed by the
Commission, however, the governing principle should be to prevent duplicate compensation or
conflicting obligations for the same megawatts in the same interval without imposing technology-
based screens unrelated to the service delivered.

        Subject to the express eligibility limits in PURA §39.170(b)(3), LLDMS should be defined
by what ERCOT receives-verified megawatts of demand reduction, available and deliverable on
instruction during the obligation period. A resource that delivers the defined service and satisfies
the pre-qualification and verification requirements should be compensated on equal terms at the
clearing price. Eligibility should not turn on a resource' s operating characteristics or on the ease
with which a particular resource class provides the service, except where those characteristics bear
on an express statutory eligibility restriction or the resource' s ability to perform. A competitive
procurement exists precisely to select the resources with the lowest opportunity cost of curtailment;
technology-based exclusions unrelated to eligibility or performance can reduce competition and
increase the clearing price paid by load serving entities-and ultimately consumers-for the same
reliability product.

        The energy market supplies the controlling analogy. Energy is compensated at the clearing
price for every resource that delivers it. A solar facility is not paid less at midday because sunshine
makes energy "easier" for it to produce than for a thermal unit; the market captures the benefit of
low-cost production through the clearing price itself, which low-cost offers discipline downward.
If the Commission or ERCOT finds itself constructing eligibility screens to avoid paying certain
resources for a service they demonstrably provide, that is not evidence the resources should be
excluded-it is evidence the service is incorrectly defined. The remedy is to define the service
correctly: specify the product (verified, incremental demand reduction available on instruction),
specify the baseline and verification rules that establish incrementality, and pay every qualifying




             Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 9 of 22
 resource that delivers it. TBGA's recommendation R-7 (Section III.F) supplies the incrementality
rule that makes resource-type screens unnecessary.

       TBGA accordingly recommends that the Commission state in the preamble to the adopted
rule, and reflect in any review of ERCOT' s implementing rules under § 25.521(i), that the
statutory exclusions required by PURA §39.170(b)(3) are applied according to their terms and that
any additional §25.521(c)(2) exclusions are narrowly tailored to prevent duplicate compensation
or conflicting obligations for the same megawatts in the same interval and               applied on a
technology-neutral basis.

D.     § 25.521(d)(3)(B)(iii) - Automatic offer rejection should be harmonized with the
       compliance framework in subsection (g). (R-5)

       Proposed § 25.521(d)(3)(B)(iii) requires ERCOT to reject any offer "submitted on behalf
of a large load customer that failed to comply with ERCOT instructions to deploy during the
previous LLDMS obligation period." As drafted, this is a one-strike disqualification with no
materiality threshold, no opportunity to cure, and no lookback limit-and it operates automatically,
outside the compliance framework in subsection (g), which requires ERCOT to establish criteria
for payment reduction, clawback, suspension, and reinstatement. The two provisions are redundant
at best and contradictory at worst: subsection (g)(2) expressly contemplates that a suspended
customer can be reinstated, while (d)(3)(B)(iii) would bar the same customer' s offers indefinitely
for a single instance of nonperformance of any magnitude.

       The consequences of nonperformance matter-TBGA' s entire Section III.A rests on
dependable performance-but consequences should be proportionate, defined, and administered
through one framework. A customer that under-delivers by 2 MW on a 200 MW obligation because
of an equipment fault, reports the event, and cures it should be treated differently from a customer
that ignores a deployment instruction. Subsection (g). The criteria under subsection (g) should be
established prospectively and should address materiality, notice of the asserted deficiency and
supporting data, a reasonable opportunity to respond and cure where appropriate, partial
performance, documented circumstances outside the customer' s reasonable control, proportional
remedies, reinstatement, and a defined process for contesting a payment reduction, clawback, or
suspension. Proposed rule text appears in Section V.




           Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 10 of 22
 E.     § 25.521(e) - Restoration is part of reliable performance. (R-8)

       Proposed § 25.521(e)(3)(B) requires a deployed customer to remain deployed "until the
large load customer can be recalled safely, as determined and communicated by ERCOT." That is
the rule' s only reference to restoration, and it is one-directional. Curtailment is not complete
merely because load has been reduced; safe restoration is part of reliable performance, and
uncoordinated load rebound at the end of an emergency is itself a system risk. Large flexible loads
can ramp back in controlled increments, but only if the recall procedure defines sequencing, ramp
expectations, and communication in advance. TBGA recommends a new § 25.521(e)(4) requiring
ERCOT and the serving utility to coordinate recall and restoration with the deployed customer,
consistent with the restoration procedures in the rules developed under subsection (a). Proposed
rule text appears in Section V.

F.     § 25.521(f) - Payment must be certain for performance, and LLDMS compensation
       must remain distinct from the subsection (a)(1) obligation. (R-6, R-7)

       Two changes to subsection (f) are needed. First, proposed § 25.521(f)(1)(C) and (f)(1)(D)
provide that a qualified scheduling entity ("QSE") "may receive" payment-permissive language
that leaves payment discretionary even for a customer in full compliance with its obligations. No
customer should commit firm curtailment capability, forgo revenue during an obligation period,
and deploy on instruction against a payment obligation that is optional on its face. Both provisions
should read "must receive.' Second, § 25.521(f)(1)(C) states no quantity basis for the availability
payment: 25% of the market clearing price multiplied by what quantity, over what hours? Section
IV, Question 1, below proposes the formula; the rule text should state it.

       Separately, the Commission should preserve-with precision-the distinction between the
two components of PURA § 39.170 that the proposed rule implements. Firm-load-shed capability
under § 25.521(a)(1) is an uncompensated, interconnection-related backstop exercised during firm
load shed. LLDMS under § 25.521(a)(2) and (c)-(f) is a compensated reliability service procured
and deployed before firm load shed, precisely so that firm load shed is avoided. A customer should
not receive LLDMS compensation for demand reduction that ERCOT is already entitled to receive
at the time of deployment-for example, reduction required at that time by a transitional
curtailment condition applicable to the customer' s interconnection, an interconnection or service




           Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 11 of 22
 agreement, a utility tariff, an ancillary service award, or another compensated demand-response
arrangement.

       The temporal qualifier-"at the time of deployment"-is essential. Every load covered by
subsection (a)(1) is required to be curtailable during firm load shed; if that standing capability
alone defeated LLDMS compensation, the newest and most flexible loads on the system would be
categorically excluded from the program, and LLDMS would procure nothing from the fleet best
able to provide it. The correct principle is that the subsection (a)(1) obligation attaches during firm
load shed, LLDMS deployment occurs before and instead of firm load shed, and the two therefore
do not overlap: LLDMS compensates reduction ERCOT is not otherwise entitled to receive when
it issues the deployment instruction. TBGA recommends codifying this as new § 25.521(f)(5).
Proposed rule text appears in Section V.

G.     § 25.521(c)(2), (f), and (i) - The Commission should rationalize LLDMS with the
       Emergency Response Service and eliminate duplicative ratepayer cost. (R-9)

       The proposed rule creates a second emergency demand response program alongside one
that has operated in ERCOT for more than a decade. Under 16 TAC § 25.507, ERCOT procures
Emergency Response Service from qualified loads and unregistered dispatchable generators,
including aggregations, represented by QSEs, that make themselves available for deployment
within ten to thirty minutes to help prevent or alleviate an actual or anticipated EEA event-the
same operative purpose stated in proposed § 25.521(d). ERS is procured competitively across four
standard contract terms, compensates resources for availability, is subj ect to an annual expenditure
cap, authorizes ERCOT to reject offers that are unreasonable or outside the parameters of an
acceptable offer, imposes suspension and reinstatement procedures, and requires an annual
effectiveness report to the Commission each April 15 under § 25.507(g). Every one of those
elements has a direct counterpart in proposed § 25.521; the proposed rule borrows the § 25.507
offer-rejection standard nearly verbatim. The Commission is, in substance, standing up a parallel
ERS for large loads.

       The proposed rule itself acknowledges the overlap: § 25.521(c)(2)(A) through (C) make
the two programs mutually exclusive for any given customer. But mutual exclusivity solves only
half of the problem. It prevents ERCOT from paying one load twice; it does not prevent ratepayers
from funding the same insurance twice at the program level. With both programs in place, load-



            Comments of the Texas Bitcoin & GRID Alliance - Project No. 58482 - Page 12 of 22
 serving entities-and ultimately consumers-fund up to $54 million ofLLDMS procurement and
up to $75 million of ERS procurement (up to $100 million when ERCOT exercises its $25 million
contract-renewal authority under § 25.507): as much as $154 million per year for two programs
procuring substantially the same product, before any ancillary service costs. Consistent with
TBGA's commitment to residential ratepayers stated in Section I, that duplication deserves a
deliberate answer, not an accident of sequential rulemakings.

       The programs are not identical, and the differences define the transition question. ERS
provides ten- and thirty-minute response deployed within an emergency, from a fleet that includes
loads below 75 MW, aggregations, and small generators that LLDMS cannot reach; LLDMS
provides larger blocks of reduction on 24-hour notice, deployed before the emergency arrives. But
the direction of travel runs one way. Loads of 75 MW and above are the fastest-growing resource
class on the ERCOT system, every megawatt enrolled in LLDMS deploys earlier in the event
sequence than ERS, and each such megawatt reduces the probability that ERS is ever needed. As
LLDMS enrollment grows, the incremental reliability value of ERS shrinks while its budget
remains fixed-the defining profile of a program that should be reduced, consolidated, or retired.

       TBGA recommends that the Commission choose the endpoint deliberately rather than carry
both programs indefinitely. The logical options are: (1) consolidate ERS into LLDMS and repeal
§ 25.507 once LLDMS is operational at scale; (2) maintain ERS at a significantly reduced budget,
limited to the resources LLDMS cannot reach; or (3) phase ERS down on a schedule keyed to
LLDMS enrollment. At a minimum, the Commission should adopt new § 25.521(j), proposed in
Section V, requiring ERCOT to evaluate the two programs jointly each year-in conjunction with
the existing April 15 ERS report under § 25.507(g)-including the megawatts and dollars procured
under each, the overlap in the reliability need served, the ERS procurement that LLDMS
enrollment has made unnecessary, and a recommendation on reduction, consolidation, or phase-
out. Ratepayers should pay for emergency demand response once, sized to the need.

                IV.     RESPONSES TO THE COMMISSION'S QUESTIONS

Q-1:   Should a large load customer that is available but not instructed to deploy be
       compensated some percentage of the market clearing price, and if so, what is an
       appropriate payment?

       Yes, and the reason follows from the economics of the obligation itself. A load
participating in LLDMS must remain energized and consuming throughout the obligation period
so that it is available for ERCOT-directed deployment-and the obligation period, by design,
coincides with the hours in which real-time energy prices are at or near their highest. Those are
precisely the hours in which a price-responsive large load would otherwise curtail voluntarily to
avoid consuming at scarcity prices. LLDMS therefore converts curtailment from an economic
choice into an ERCOT-controlled option, and the participating customer bears the cost of
consuming at scarcity-level prices unless and until it is instructed to deploy. The availability
payment exists to blunt that exposure. Without it, every participant must internalize the full
expected cost of forced consumption at scarcity prices into its offer, inflating the LLDMS clearing
price; with it, offers can be lower and the program procures more megawatts per budget dollar.

       This economic function also identifies the price to which the percentage should apply. The
proposed text pays 25% of "the market clearing price," which could refer either to the LLDMS
procurement clearing price under § 25.521(f)(1)(A) orto the real-time energy price; the rule should
say which. TBGA recommends the real-time energy price at the customer's load zone or settlement
point during verified available hours, because that is the exposure the payment offsets-and
indexing to the energy price self-scales the payment to the incentive it is designed to counteract:
modest when prices are moderate, larger precisely when the incentive to trip is strongest. TBGA
supports the proposed 25% as a starting point, subject to three conditions: availability must be
verified through telemetry or meter data consistent with ERCOT rules, not attestation; the rule
must state the quantity basis-availability payment equals 25% x the real-time energy price
($/MWh) x the customer' s committed megawatts x the hours of the obligation period in which
availability is verified; and the percentage should be expressly revisable on the record developed
through the after-action reports required under § 25.521(h).

       PURA §39.170(b)(3) expressly prohibits participation by a large load customer that curtails
in response to the wholesale price of electricity, as determined by ERCOT. The rule therefore
should not create a pathway for an LLDMS participant to opt out of its availability obligation

 because wholesale prices rise. It should, however, distinguish price-responsive curtailment from
documented temporary unavailability caused by a safety condition, equipment failure, interruption
of utility service, or another non-price-responsive circumstance recognized in ERCOT protocols.
A customer should not receive an availability payment for hours in which its committed demand
reduction is unavailable, and any resulting nonperformance should be addressed proportionately
under subsection (g). Proposed rule text appears in Section V as revised § 25.521(e)(5).

Q-2:   What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program (proposed maximum of $54
       million per calendar year)?

       The Commission should treat the budget as an output of the risk assessment required by §
25.521(d)(2), not as an independent input, and should require full transparency on how the budget
is consumed. The arithmetic shows why. At the $5,000/MWh offer cap in § 25.521(d)(3)(B)(v),
$54 million purchases 10,800 MWh of deployed reduction-approximately one deployment of
1,000 MW sustained for eleven hours at the cap. At a more realistic $1,000/MWh clearing price,
the budget supports 54,000 MWh of deployment. Availability payments draw on the same budget
and can consume it with zero deployments: under the formula proposed in response to Question 1,
a commitment of 2,000 MW for a 720-hour monthly obligation period at a $100/MWh average
real-time energy price yields availability payments of 25% x $100 x 2,000 MW x 720 hours == $36
million-two-thirds of the annual budget for a single month of standing availability.

       TBGA accordingly recommends: (1) the rule should state expressly whether availability
payments count against the annual cap; (2) the quantity ERCOT procures should continue to be
governed by the § 25.521(d)(2) risk assessment, with the budget sized to that assessment rather
than the assessment truncated to the budget; and (3) the § 25.521(h) after-action report should be
expanded to state budget consumption to date and any procurement forgone because of the cap, so
that the Commission can revisit the cap on an evidentiary record rather than an assumption; and
(4) the budget should be evaluated jointly with ERS expenditures under 16 TAC § 25.507, as
discussed in Section III.G, so that combined ratepayer-funded emergency demand response
spending-up to $129 million per year across the two programs, and up to $154 million with ERS
renewal authority-is sized to the reliability need once, not twice.

 Q-3:   What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition, and how
       far in advance should ERCOT start the auction?

       Procurement timing should follow forecast skill. Weather forecast accuracy degrades
materially beyond one to two weeks; procuring a month ahead on the § 25.521(d)(1)(A) monthly
probabilistic assessment buys expensive insurance against forecasts that will frequently be wrong
in both directions-committing budget when no event materializes, and under-procuring when one
does. TBGA recommends that the weekly forecast trigger in § 25.521(d)(1)(B) serve as the
primary procurement pathway, with the monthly probabilistic assessment functioning as a
screening and readiness layer rather than a procurement commitment. The annual pre-qualification
structure in § 25.521(c) makes compressed auction timelines practical: because participants are
pre-qualified and represented by QSEs year-round, ERCOT can issue a request for proposal and
clear an auction within 24 to 72 hours of identifying an elevated risk, procuring as close to the
obligation period as operational needs allow. Flexible large loads do not require long mobilization
lead times; the auction should be run when the forecast is good enough to size it correctly.

       The precondition for that short cadence is a product that is standardized, well defined, and
understandable in advance. Long procurement lead times exist to give participants time to plan
and manage around a period of risk-to purchase hedging products, arrange other risk-
management tools, or install equipment. None of that is needed here. LLDMS is a simple
curtailment product: a pre-qualified load, represented by a QSE, offers a known quantity of
demand reduction at a price and curtails on instruction. Every element that genuinely requires lead
time-pre-qualification, the price-responsive test, telemetry, registration, and the LLDMS
agreement-is completed annually in advance under § 25.521(c), so the only variables remaining
at auction time are price and quantity. It is therefore critical that the rule and ERCOT's
implementing rules under § 25.521(i) be comprehensive and clear before the first request for
proposal issues: the obligation period, availability verification, deployment and recall terms, the
payment basis, and the consequences of nonperformance must all be fixed in advance, so that a
participant can evaluate an RFP and respond within hours rather than negotiate terms within them.
A well-defined product enables a fast market; an ambiguous one forces the lead time back in.

 Q-4:   Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies, and with
       what limitations?

       Yes, with defined limits. TBGA first notes a drafting anomaly: "transmission emergency"
is defined in § 25.521(b)(4) but appears nowhere in the operative procurement or deployment
provisions of subsections (d) and (e), which are limited to EEA events driven by extreme weather.
If the Commission intends transmission-emergency deployment, conforming amendments are
required to make the defined term operative; if not, the definition should be deleted.

       On the merits, a transmission emergency as defined-an element operating above its
emergency rating creating significant risk of firm load shed-is precisely the condition in which
targeted, voluntary, compensated load reduction is most valuable, because a small quantity of
megawatts in the right electrical location can resolve a constraint that would otherwise force firm
load shed on the same area. TBGA recommends authorizing transmission-emergency deployment
subject to six limitations: (l) ERCOT may deploy LLDMS for a transmission emergency only
after it has exhausted the other mechanisms available to manage the constraint-including
security-constrained economic dispatch and redispatch, transmission reconfiguration, and
applicable remedial action or mitigation plans-so that LLDMS remains the tool of last resort
before firm load shed, not a substitute for ordinary congestion management; (2) LLDMS must
never be deployed to facilitate or accommodate a planned generation or transmission outage-a
planned outage is a scheduling decision, not an emergency, and using a compensated reliability
service to enable outage coordination would convert an emergency backstop into a subsidy for
outage scheduling, paid by load-serving entities; (3) ERCOT may deploy only large load
customers whose reduction is electrically effective for the constrained element or interface; (4) the
notice, deployment, and recall provisions of § 25.521(e) apply equally, including the 24-hour
notice requirement; (5) transmission-emergency deployments count against the annual budget and
are settled under subsection (f) on the same terms; and (6) each transmission-emergency
deployment is reported under § 25.521(h), including identification of the constraint, the
effectiveness basis for the loads deployed, and the alternative mechanisms exhausted before
deployment.

                                        VI.     CONCLUSION

       Texas can accommodate substantial large load growth without treating flexibility as a
vague or voluntary concept. The relevant standard is not whether a customer says it can curtail; it
is whether ERCOT can depend upon the required capability when system conditions require it.
TBGA's members operate the most flexible large loads on the ERCOT system and volunteer for
the most rigorous version of that standard: capability that is physical, measurable, tested,
verifiable, and enforceable; clear, prospective treatment of post-2025 incremental load that
respects the statute' s date limitation; eligibility and compensation rules defined by the service
delivered rather than the resource delivering it, subj ect to express statutory restrictions; and
payment that is certain for performance. TBGA respectfully requests that the Commission adopt
the recommendations set out above and the rule text proposed in Section V.
